title: Zuriel Theological Comparisons — Christian Interpretations in Context
description: A balanced introductory guide to selected doctrinal questions, representative Christian interpretations, biblical passages and historical context. It is not a substitute for Scripture, a local church's confessional documents or specialist theological study.
editorialPolicy: Present traditions fairly and distinguish shared convictions from genuine disagreements.
Traditions are internally diverse; the summaries describe broad tendencies, not every church or believer.
Scripture references are starting points and must be read in their literary and historical contexts.
Do not imply that every view has equal historical prevalence or that a short summary settles a debate.
Distinguish explicit biblical statements, theological inference, church tradition and later terminology.
Use respectful language; do not mock, caricature or label whole Christian communities by a disputed position.

entries.title: Salvation, grace and justification
entries.question: How are grace, faith, justification, transformation and good works related?
entries.sharedGround: Historic Christian traditions affirm that salvation depends on God's grace and the saving work of Jesus Christ, not on human boasting. They also affirm that genuine faith is meant to shape a transformed life.

positions.summary: Many Lutheran and Reformed traditions describe justification as God's gracious declaration received through faith, while insisting that good works follow as the fruit of living faith. Wesleyan traditions emphasise prevenient grace and a faith that works through love.
positions.traditions: Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Baptist, Methodist and other Protestant traditions; formulations differ.

positions.summary: Catholic teaching describes justification as originating in God's grace, involving forgiveness and inner renewal, received through faith and baptism and lived out in hope and love. Good works are responses enabled by grace, not independent self-salvation.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic Church; consult its catechism and official teaching for the full formulation.

positions.summary: Orthodox theology often frames salvation through participation in God's life (theosis), healing and transformation. It emphasises grace, faith, sacramental life and cooperation with divine grace, while resisting a narrow separation between legal status and renewal.
positions.traditions: Eastern Orthodox churches; emphases and explanations vary among theologians.

entries.historicalContext: The Reformation-era debates sharpened disagreements about justification, merit, assurance and the relation of faith to works. Earlier Christian writers used several overlapping biblical images for salvation, including forgiveness, adoption, healing, victory and participation in Christ.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: The traditions differ over the precise meaning of justification, the role of sacraments, imputed and imparted righteousness, assurance and how to describe cooperation with grace. Avoid reducing the disagreement to 'grace versus works'.
entries.readingCaution: Read Ephesians 2:8-10 as a whole: salvation is by grace, and the saved are created for good works. Compare Romans and James in their distinct arguments.

entries.title: Baptism: infants, believers and its meaning
entries.question: Who should be baptised, and what does baptism signify or accomplish?
entries.sharedGround: Most historic Christian communities regard baptism as a command of Christ and a public, ecclesial act closely connected with discipleship, repentance, faith and entry into the Christian community.

positions.summary: Baptist and many evangelical churches baptise those who personally profess faith, commonly by immersion, viewing baptism as a sign of union with Christ and public confession.
positions.traditions: Baptist, many Pentecostal and independent evangelical churches.

positions.summary: Reformed and some other Protestant churches baptise infants of believing households, understanding baptism in relation to God's covenant promises and the visible church; personal faith is expected as the child matures.
positions.traditions: Presbyterian and some Reformed, Anglican, Lutheran and Methodist communities, with different sacramental understandings.

positions.summary: Catholic, Orthodox and some Protestant traditions teach that baptism is a means through which God gives grace and incorporates a person into Christ and the Church. Infant baptism is ordinarily practised, with later formation in faith.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican and Methodist traditions, though their sacramental theology differs.

entries.historicalContext: Infant baptism is attested early in Christian history, while believer's baptism is prominent in the New Testament narratives and became a central issue in the Radical Reformation and later Baptist movements. The meaning of household baptisms is debated.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Disagreements include the proper recipients, mode, timing, relation to regeneration, covenant continuity and whether baptism is primarily sign, sacrament or both.
entries.readingCaution: Do not use a single household narrative as if it answered every question. Compare narrative accounts with apostolic teaching and the whole biblical context.

entries.title: The Lord's Supper / Communion
entries.question: How is Christ present in Communion, and what does the meal communicate?
entries.sharedGround: Christians broadly agree that the Supper was instituted by Jesus, proclaims His death, calls the church to remembrance and thanksgiving, and expresses communion among believers.

positions.summary: Catholic teaching holds that the substance of bread and wine becomes Christ's Body and Blood while the appearances remain. The Eucharist is understood as sacrificial memorial and real participation in Christ.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic Church.

positions.summary: Lutheran teaching confesses that Christ's true Body and Blood are genuinely present and received with the bread and wine, without adopting the Roman explanation of transubstantiation.
positions.traditions: Lutheran churches.

positions.summary: Many Reformed traditions teach that believers truly commune with Christ spiritually by the Holy Spirit through faith, while the bread and cup remain bread and wine.
positions.traditions: Reformed and Presbyterian traditions; accounts vary.

positions.summary: Many Baptist, Pentecostal and other free-church communities emphasise remembrance, proclamation and obedient participation, while some also speak of spiritual nourishment and communion with Christ.
positions.traditions: Many Baptist, Pentecostal and independent evangelical churches.

entries.historicalContext: The early church treated the Eucharist as central worship. Medieval Western theology developed the term transubstantiation; the sixteenth-century Reformation produced several distinct accounts of Christ's presence and the Supper's function.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Christ's mode of presence, the relation of the Supper to sacrifice, the role of ordained ministry, frequency and who may participate are debated.
entries.readingCaution: Read 1 Corinthians 10-11 in its setting of church unity, idolatry, self-examination and care for poorer members; do not reduce the passage to a debate over elements alone.

entries.title: Spiritual gifts: continuation and cessation
entries.question: Do miraculous and revelatory gifts continue in the church today?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm the Holy Spirit's active work, the need for discernment, the centrality of love and the authority of Scripture.

positions.summary: Continuationists believe the gifts described in the New Testament, including prophecy, healing and tongues, remain available to the church, subject to biblical testing, order and love.
positions.traditions: Pentecostal, charismatic and many evangelical communities.

positions.summary: Cessationists generally hold that certain sign or revelatory gifts served a foundational apostolic role and are not normative in the same way today, while affirming the Spirit's ongoing work and providence.
positions.traditions: Some Reformed, evangelical and Baptist communities; positions vary in scope.

positions.summary: Some Christians remain open to extraordinary gifts while stressing careful testing, or distinguish between the continuation of gifts and claims to new authoritative doctrine.
positions.traditions: Various Anglican, Methodist, evangelical and non-denominational communities.

entries.historicalContext: The question has been discussed throughout church history, but modern Pentecostal and charismatic movements brought it into renewed prominence from the twentieth century onward. Different traditions interpret 1 Corinthians 13 and the apostolic foundation texts differently.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Disagreement concerns the purpose and duration of particular gifts, the meaning of 'the perfect', how prophecy should be evaluated, and how to distinguish genuine gifts from error or manipulation.
entries.readingCaution: No claimed gift should override Scripture, coerce people, demand money or prevent medical care. Read Paul's instructions on order, testing and love alongside any discussion of gifts.

entries.title: Predestination, election and human response
entries.question: How does God's initiative relate to human freedom and responsibility?
entries.sharedGround: Historic Christian traditions affirm God's sovereignty, the priority of grace, the reality of human responsibility and the call to repent and believe.

positions.summary: These accounts stress God's gracious initiative and election, often teaching that saving faith is itself the result of God's effective grace. Reformed theologians differ in how they explain the relation of election, human willing and the scope of atonement.
positions.traditions: Reformed and some Augustinian Protestant traditions.

positions.summary: These accounts stress prevenient grace, by which God enables a genuine human response, and understand election in relation to God's foreknowledge of faith or participation in Christ, depending on the tradition.
positions.traditions: Wesleyan, Methodist, many Pentecostal and Arminian evangelical communities.

positions.summary: Catholic and Orthodox approaches affirm that grace always comes first and that human response matters. They generally resist accounts that make God the author of evil or erase meaningful human cooperation, while differing internally on technical explanations.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions; neither is a single simplified theory.

entries.historicalContext: The debate reaches back to Augustine and later intensified through medieval theology, the Reformation, the Remonstrant controversy and Wesleyan revival movements. Christian thinkers have used different philosophical terms to describe freedom and providence.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Key differences concern unconditional election, prevenient or resistible grace, the meaning of foreknowledge, perseverance, and how to read Romans 9 alongside universal invitations and warnings.
entries.readingCaution: Do not isolate Romans 9 from Romans 10-11. Read election texts alongside passages that call people to respond, and avoid claiming to know the eternal state of particular individuals.

entries.title: Church leadership and governance
entries.question: How should authority and oversight be organised in the church?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm qualified leadership, pastoral care, accountability, service, sound teaching and the shared responsibility of the whole body.

positions.summary: Bishops exercise oversight across congregations, usually alongside presbyters and deacons. Supporters point to early patterns of regional oversight and continuity in teaching and ministry.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican, Methodist and other episcopal churches, with significant differences.

positions.summary: Elders share oversight through local sessions and wider councils or presbyteries. Authority is exercised collegially rather than concentrated in a single diocesan bishop.
positions.traditions: Presbyterian and some Reformed churches.

positions.summary: The local congregation has substantial authority in membership, discipline, calling leaders and major decisions, often with elders or pastors serving within congregational accountability.
positions.traditions: Many Baptist, Congregationalist and independent churches.

entries.historicalContext: The New Testament uses several leadership terms, including elder, overseer and deacon. The historical development of episcopacy, presbyteries and congregational autonomy occurred over centuries and in varied regional settings.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Disputes concern apostolic succession, the authority of bishops, ordination, local autonomy, the role of councils and how discipline should be exercised.
entries.readingCaution: No governance model permits spiritual abuse or unaccountable control. Read leadership texts with Jesus' teaching that authority is exercised through service.

entries.title: The millennium and Christ's return
entries.question: How should Revelation 20 and other end-time passages be understood?
entries.sharedGround: Historic Christian traditions confess Christ's return, final judgement, resurrection and the renewal of creation. They disagree about the sequence and symbolism of particular prophetic passages.

positions.summary: Christ returns before the millennium described in Revelation 20. Historic premillennial and dispensational premillennial accounts differ on Israel, the church and the timing of tribulation events.
positions.traditions: Found in various evangelical, Baptist, Pentecostal and other communities.

positions.summary: The millennium is read symbolically as the present reign of Christ with His saints, with the final return, resurrection and judgement bringing history to its consummation.
positions.traditions: Common in Augustinian, Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and many Reformed interpretations, though not universally held within them.

positions.summary: Christ returns after an extended era in which the gospel's influence brings widespread flourishing or righteousness, while interpretations differ over how literally to understand the millennium.
positions.traditions: Held by some Reformed and other Protestant theologians, historically and today.

entries.historicalContext: Early Christian writers held more than one expectation about the millennium. Augustine's influential symbolic interpretation shaped much Western theology, while premillennial and postmillennial readings continued in various movements.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: The debate concerns the literary genre of Revelation, the relation of Israel and the church, the binding of Satan, tribulation, resurrection chronology and the nature of the millennium.
entries.readingCaution: Avoid date-setting and fear-based predictions. Apocalyptic imagery should be read in its literary context and alongside the clear call to faithfulness, hope and endurance.

entries.title: Women, ministry and church leadership
entries.question: How should biblical teaching about women and men in ministry be interpreted?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm the equal dignity of women and men before God and recognise women's significant participation in biblical ministry, discipleship, witness and service.

positions.summary: These interpretations affirm equal worth while holding that certain governing or teaching offices in the gathered church are reserved for qualified men. They differ over which roles are restricted and how relevant passages apply today.
positions.traditions: Many conservative evangelical, Baptist, Reformed and other churches.

positions.summary: These interpretations hold that leadership and teaching gifts should be recognised without restriction based on sex, reading restrictive passages in their local historical setting and alongside women who lead, teach or serve in Scripture.
positions.traditions: Many Methodist, Anglican, Pentecostal, Baptist and other Protestant churches.

positions.view: Traditions with male priesthood and broad women's ministries
positions.summary: Catholic and Orthodox churches reserve priestly ordination to men while recognising extensive forms of women's theological, charitable, educational and spiritual leadership; their rationales and practices differ.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.

entries.historicalContext: Christian communities have interpreted Paul's instructions, the ministries of women in the New Testament and the development of church offices in different ways. Modern debates are shaped by historical study, ecclesiology and changing social contexts.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Differences concern the scope of apostolic restrictions, the meaning of headship and authority, the examples of women leaders, ordination and the distinction between spiritual gifts and church office.
entries.readingCaution: Do not use this topic to justify abuse, silence victims or deny anyone's dignity. Read disputed passages in their immediate context and alongside the whole biblical witness.

entries.title: Sabbath, Sunday and Christian rest
entries.question: How do Christians understand the seventh-day Sabbath and the Lord's Day?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm the importance of worship, rest, gathered fellowship and trust in God rather than endless work or self-reliance.

positions.summary: Seventh-day Sabbatarians maintain that the seventh day remains the biblical Sabbath and should be kept as a day of rest and worship, while differing in their wider theological explanations.
positions.traditions: Seventh-day Adventist and other Sabbatarian communities.

positions.view: Sunday as the Christian Lord's Day
positions.summary: Many Christians regard Sunday, the day associated with Jesus' resurrection and early Christian gathering, as the principal weekly day for worship and rest, sometimes understanding it as the Christian Sabbath.
positions.traditions: Many Reformed, Anglican, Baptist, Methodist and other churches, with different levels of Sabbath obligation.

positions.summary: Other Christians emphasise that no particular day should be imposed as a universal covenant requirement for believers, while affirming regular worship and rhythms of rest.
positions.traditions: Various Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, evangelical and free-church interpretations.

entries.historicalContext: The earliest Christians were largely Jewish and lived amid Sabbath practice, while New Testament writings also describe first-day gatherings. The relationship between Sabbath commandment, resurrection worship and Christian liberty developed differently across traditions.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Disagreements include whether the fourth commandment transfers to Sunday, the binding force of Mosaic covenant law, the role of tradition and how Romans 14 and Colossians 2 apply.
entries.readingCaution: Do not treat another believer's day of worship as proof of their spiritual standing. Read the Sabbath command in its creation, exodus and covenant settings.

entries.title: The meaning of the atonement
entries.question: How do biblical images explain what Christ accomplished through His death and resurrection?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm that Jesus' death and resurrection reconcile humanity to God, defeat sin and death, reveal divine love and are central to salvation.

positions.summary: This account emphasises that Christ bears sin's judgement on behalf of sinners, satisfying divine justice and bringing forgiveness and reconciliation. Christian theologians explain its relation to other atonement images in different ways.
positions.traditions: Prominent in many Reformed and evangelical Protestant traditions.

positions.summary: This account emphasises Christ's victory over sin, death and the powers of evil through His incarnation, cross and resurrection. It is often presented as a major biblical theme alongside other explanations.
positions.traditions: Prominent in patristic, Orthodox and many contemporary Protestant accounts.

positions.summary: These approaches stress that Christ enters human suffering, heals human nature, restores communion with God and transforms believers through participation in His life and self-giving love.
positions.traditions: Important in Eastern Orthodox, Catholic and a range of Protestant theologians.

positions.summary: This account highlights how the cross reveals God's love and moves people toward repentance, reconciliation and self-giving discipleship. Many theologians treat this as one biblical dimension rather than the only explanation.
positions.traditions: Found in several historical and contemporary Christian traditions.

entries.historicalContext: The New Testament uses several images for Christ's saving work: sacrifice, ransom, reconciliation, justification, victory, cleansing, adoption and example. Early, medieval and Reformation theologians developed different accounts that often overlap rather than exclude one another.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Debates concern the meaning of divine justice, substitution, sacrifice, victory, the role of human transformation and whether one model should be treated as the controlling explanation.
entries.readingCaution: Avoid forcing every biblical image into one formula. Read each passage on its own terms and consider how the different images together describe Christ's saving work.

entries.title: The Trinity and the identity of God
entries.question: How do Christians understand the Father, Son and Holy Spirit in relation to the one God?
entries.sharedGround: Historic Nicene Christianity confesses one God and identifies the Father, Son and Holy Spirit as divine. Christians who use different formulations must be described accurately rather than treated as though all positions are the same.

positions.summary: One God exists eternally as three distinct, co-equal and co-eternal Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Persons are not three gods, nor are they merely three temporary roles or appearances.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and most Protestant churches.

positions.summary: Emphasises the absolute oneness of God and understands Father, Son and Spirit through God's self-revelation and saving work in Jesus Christ, rather than three eternal divine Persons.
positions.traditions: Oneness Pentecostal denominations and fellowships.

positions.summary: Some groups understand Jesus as distinct from and subordinate to the one God, or understand the Holy Spirit as God's power or presence rather than a distinct divine Person. These positions differ substantially from one another.
positions.traditions: Various nontrinitarian movements; their teachings should be described individually.

entries.historicalContext: The early church debated how to speak faithfully about Jesus' divinity and the Spirit while maintaining biblical monotheism. The Nicene Creed and later pro-Nicene theology established the Trinitarian language used by most historic Christian traditions.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Disagreement concerns the meaning of person and being, the eternal relation of the Son to the Father, the deity and personhood of the Spirit, and how biblical language should be synthesised.
entries.readingCaution: Do not use analogies such as water, ice and steam as complete explanations; they can imply that God merely changes modes. Read passages about the Father, Son and Spirit together, while distinguishing biblical wording from later theological terminology.

entries.title: Baptism in the Holy Spirit
entries.question: Is baptism in the Holy Spirit distinct from conversion, and how is it evidenced?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm that the Holy Spirit gives new life, unites believers to Christ, empowers witness and produces holy character. All should test spiritual claims by Scripture and their fruit.

positions.summary: Many classical Pentecostals teach a distinct experience of baptism in the Holy Spirit, ordinarily subsequent to conversion, empowering witness and commonly associated with speaking in tongues as initial physical evidence.
positions.traditions: Classical Pentecostal denominations; details differ among them.

positions.summary: Many charismatics affirm ongoing Spirit baptism or fresh fillings and empowerments, but differ on whether it is a distinct post-conversion experience and whether tongues are a necessary initial sign.
positions.traditions: Charismatic Catholics, Anglicans, evangelicals and independent churches.

positions.summary: Many Reformed, Lutheran, Baptist and other Christians understand Spirit baptism primarily as the Spirit's once-for-all incorporation of believers into Christ at conversion, while affirming repeated fillings and empowerment.
positions.traditions: Many non-Pentecostal Protestant traditions.

entries.historicalContext: The modern Pentecostal movement brought renewed attention to Acts' accounts of Spirit empowerment in the early twentieth century. Later charismatic renewal spread spiritual-gifts discussion across many church traditions.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Key questions include whether Acts describes a repeatable pattern or unique stages in the church's beginning, how 1 Corinthians 12:13 relates to Acts, and whether tongues are universal evidence or one gift among many.
entries.readingCaution: Do not judge a believer's salvation or worth by whether they speak in tongues. Distinguish the Spirit's indwelling, filling, gifts and fruit, and read narrative passages alongside the letters.

entries.title: Divine healing, suffering and prayer
entries.question: How should Christians understand healing prayer alongside illness, suffering and medical care?
entries.sharedGround: Christians affirm that God hears prayer, cares for those who suffer, and will finally bring resurrection and the restoration of creation. Compassion, practical care and hope belong together.

positions.summary: Affirms that God may heal today through prayer, gifts of healing and providential means, and encourages believers to pray expectantly while recognising that not every prayer results in immediate healing.
positions.traditions: Pentecostal and charismatic communities, with varied teaching and practice.

positions.summary: Emphasises prayer, anointing, sacraments, pastoral presence and the church's ministry to the sick. Healing may include spiritual, emotional and bodily care, without assuming that physical recovery is guaranteed.
positions.traditions: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other sacramental traditions.

positions.summary: Stresses God's sustaining presence through suffering, lament, community and medical treatment, while remaining open to extraordinary answers to prayer. Some traditions are more cautious about claims of miraculous healing.
positions.traditions: Reformed, evangelical and other Protestant communities; approaches vary.

entries.historicalContext: Healing prayer appears throughout Scripture and Christian history. Churches have developed different practices of anointing, intercession, pilgrimage, pastoral care and medical service.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Disputes concern the interpretation of Isaiah 53, the scope of healing in the atonement, the role of spiritual gifts, and how to understand unanswered prayer and suffering.
entries.readingCaution: Never tell sick or disabled people that their condition proves weak faith, hidden sin or failure to claim a promise. Prayer must not replace appropriate medical care or be used to sell guaranteed cures.

entries.title: Assurance, perseverance and falling away
entries.question: Can a believer know they are secure in Christ, and can a believer finally fall away?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions call believers to trust God's grace, continue in faith, heed biblical warnings and pursue a life shaped by Christ. Assurance should lead to hope and faithful living, not presumption or despair.

positions.view: Eternal security / perseverance of the saints
positions.summary: Many Reformed and some evangelical traditions teach that those truly regenerated by God will be preserved in faith to the end. Warnings are real means God uses to keep believers persevering, though traditions explain apparent apostasy differently.
positions.traditions: Reformed and some Baptist evangelical traditions.

positions.summary: Arminian and Wesleyan traditions commonly teach that believers are genuinely secure as they remain in Christ, while warning that persistent, deliberate rejection of faith can lead to falling away.
positions.traditions: Wesleyan, Methodist, Arminian and many Pentecostal traditions.

positions.summary: Catholic and Orthodox traditions emphasise grace, ongoing repentance, participation in the life of the Church and the seriousness of freely turning away from God. Assurance is grounded in God's mercy without claiming certainty about every future choice.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, with distinct theological frameworks.

entries.historicalContext: The relationship between grace, freedom, apostasy and perseverance was debated by early theologians and later during the Reformation and revival movements. Different readings of warning and assurance passages shaped confessional traditions.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Debates concern the meaning of genuine faith, the identity of those addressed in warning passages, whether grace can finally be resisted, and the relationship between assurance and perseverance.
entries.readingCaution: Do not use warning passages to crush tender consciences or assurance passages to excuse ongoing harm. Read promises and warnings together, and direct struggling people toward Christ, repentance and pastoral support.

entries.title: Mary, the saints and intercession
entries.question: What place do Mary and departed saints have in Christian devotion and prayer?
entries.sharedGround: Christians affirm that worship belongs to God alone, that Jesus Christ is the one mediator of salvation, and that the church is called to honour faithful witnesses and imitate their faith.

positions.summary: Catholic teaching honours Mary as the Mother of God and asks for the intercession of Mary and the saints, while distinguishing veneration from the worship due to God alone. Christ remains the unique mediator in the saving sense.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic Church.

positions.summary: Orthodox Christians venerate Mary as Theotokos and honour saints, asking for their prayers as members of the living communion in Christ. Veneration is distinguished from worship, which belongs to the Triune God.
positions.traditions: Eastern Orthodox churches.

positions.summary: Many Protestant traditions honour Mary and biblical saints as examples of faith but direct prayer to God through Christ and do not invoke departed saints, often citing the sufficiency of Christ's mediation and concerns about biblical warrant.
positions.traditions: Many Baptist, Reformed, evangelical, Pentecostal and other Protestant churches.

entries.historicalContext: Honour for martyrs and remembrance of Mary developed in early Christian worship. Later debates about images, invocation, mediation and devotional practice became major points of division during the Reformation.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Differences concern the communion of saints, the legitimacy of asking departed believers for prayer, the development of Marian doctrines, and the distinction between veneration and worship in practice.
entries.readingCaution: Represent Catholic and Orthodox teaching in its own terms rather than saying they teach that Mary replaces Jesus. Equally, do not pressure Protestants to adopt devotional practices their conscience and tradition reject.

entries.title: Final judgment, hell and the destiny of the lost
entries.question: How do Christians interpret biblical teaching about final judgment and the fate of those who reject God?
entries.sharedGround: Historic Christian traditions affirm God's justice, the reality of final judgment, the seriousness of evil and the hope that God will set creation right through Christ.

positions.summary: This historic view understands final punishment as everlasting conscious separation from God and judgment. Its defenders stress the gravity of sin and the language of eternal punishment in Scripture.
positions.traditions: Held in many Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions, though explanations differ.

positions.summary: This view holds that immortality is God's gift to the redeemed and that the finally unrepentant are ultimately destroyed rather than kept alive forever in conscious torment. Advocates emphasise biblical language of death and destruction.
positions.traditions: Some evangelical, Anglican and Adventist theologians and communities.

positions.view: Universal reconciliation as a debated hope
positions.summary: Some Christian theologians hope or argue that God's saving purpose may finally reconcile all people through Christ. This remains disputed and is not the official teaching of many historic churches; proponents differ on how they read judgment texts.
positions.traditions: A minority position among some ancient and modern theologians; not one uniform denomination-wide doctrine.

entries.historicalContext: Early Christian writers discussed judgment, punishment and restoration in different ways. Creeds affirm Christ's return and judgment but do not resolve every later debate about the duration and nature of punishment.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Debates concern the meaning of eternal language, destruction imagery, freedom, justice, the scope of Christ's victory and whether post-mortem repentance is possible.
entries.readingCaution: Do not claim certainty about the final destiny of named individuals or use hell teaching to terrorise vulnerable people. Present the range of interpretations accurately while taking biblical warnings and the call to repentance seriously.

entries.title: Creation, Genesis and the natural sciences
entries.question: How should Christians read Genesis in relation to the age of the earth and scientific accounts of origins?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm that God is Creator, creation is meaningful and dependent on God, human beings bear God's image, and the natural world is worthy of care.

positions.summary: Understand the creation days as ordinary days and generally interpret biblical genealogies and chronology as indicating a relatively recent creation. They often reject common ancestry and aspects of mainstream evolutionary theory.
positions.traditions: Some conservative evangelical, Baptist and independent Christian communities.

positions.summary: Accept an ancient universe and earth while maintaining that God directly created life or intervened in distinct ways. Interpretations of the days in Genesis vary.
positions.traditions: Some evangelical and other Christian communities.

positions.summary: Accepts the broad scientific account of cosmic and biological evolution while affirming that God is Creator and sustainer. Genesis is read with attention to its theological, literary and ancient context.
positions.traditions: Found among Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Protestant and evangelical scholars and believers.

positions.summary: Focus on the theological structure and purpose of Genesis 1, seeing its ordered days as a literary framework rather than a scientific chronology. This approach may coexist with several views of biological origins.
positions.traditions: Various biblical scholars and Christian traditions.

entries.historicalContext: Christians have interpreted Genesis through different historical and literary approaches. Modern geology, astronomy and biology intensified discussion, while Christian scholars continue to debate how scientific models and biblical interpretation relate.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Disputes include the genre and chronology of Genesis, death before the fall, Adam and Eve's historical role, common ancestry and how theological claims should relate to scientific evidence.
entries.readingCaution: Do not equate a person's salvation with one particular creation model. Distinguish what a biblical text explicitly teaches from scientific claims and interpretive conclusions; avoid presenting contested scientific assertions as settled facts.

entries.title: Icons, images and sacred art
entries.question: May Christians use images in worship and devotion, and how should the second commandment be understood?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions reject idolatry and affirm that worship belongs to God alone. Many also use art to teach Scripture, remember biblical events and beautify worship spaces.

positions.summary: Orthodox theology distinguishes veneration shown to icons from worship due to God. Icons are understood as witnesses to the incarnation and as aids to prayer, with honour directed to the person depicted rather than the material object.
positions.traditions: Eastern Orthodox churches.

positions.summary: Catholic teaching permits sacred images and distinguishes the honour given to them from adoration due to God alone. Images are intended to direct the faithful toward Christ, Mary and the saints, not to be treated as independent powers.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic Church.

positions.summary: Some Protestant traditions restrict or avoid religious images in worship, arguing that images can violate the commandment or encourage false devotion. Others permit teaching art while rejecting devotional veneration.
positions.traditions: Some Reformed, Puritan, Anabaptist and evangelical communities.

entries.historicalContext: The early church debated images, culminating in the Byzantine iconoclast controversies. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) defended the veneration of icons, while the Reformation revived disagreements about images in worship.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Debates concern the difference between worship and veneration, the implications of the incarnation, the authority of church tradition and whether devotional use of images risks idolatry.
entries.readingCaution: Do not portray every image as an idol or assume that every user of an icon worships wood or paint. Equally, do not dismiss sincere concerns about idolatry; explain the theology and practice being discussed.

entries.title: Wealth, poverty, giving and prosperity teaching
entries.question: What does Scripture teach about material blessing, generosity, poverty and Christian contentment?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm that God provides, wealth carries responsibility, generosity is commanded, exploitation is condemned and material possessions must never replace love of God and neighbour.

positions.summary: Some teachers emphasise biblical promises of provision, generosity and blessing, and may expect faith and prayer to be accompanied by material increase. This broad movement contains diverse teachings, some of which make guarantees that other Christians regard as unsupported or harmful.
positions.traditions: Certain independent charismatic and Word of Faith ministries; not representative of all Pentecostal or charismatic churches.

positions.summary: Many churches teach that possessions are entrusted by God and should be managed with gratitude, justice, generosity and care for the poor. Material success is not treated as a reliable measure of faith or divine favour.
positions.traditions: Broadly shared across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions.

positions.summary: Some Christian traditions stress simplicity, detachment from wealth, communal sharing and solidarity with the poor as important disciplines of discipleship.
positions.traditions: Monastic, Anabaptist, Franciscan and other Christian movements, with varied practice.

entries.historicalContext: The church has long debated wealth and poverty, from early Christian sharing and monastic movements to modern debates about prosperity preaching, economic justice and stewardship.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Differences concern how covenant blessings apply today, the meaning of prosperity texts, the role of giving, economic justice and whether material wealth should be expected as a result of faith.
entries.readingCaution: Never promise that a donation guarantees healing, wealth or a miracle. Do not blame poor people for their circumstances or use Scripture to pressure vulnerable believers into giving beyond their means.

entries.title: The kingdom of God: present reality and future hope
entries.question: Is the kingdom of God present now, future, or both?
entries.sharedGround: Christians affirm that Jesus announced God's kingdom, that His reign calls people to repentance and faithful living, and that God's purposes will be fully revealed when Christ returns.

positions.summary: Many theologians teach that God's kingdom has been inaugurated through Jesus' ministry, death and resurrection, is experienced by the Spirit and church now, and awaits its full public completion at Christ's return.
positions.traditions: Widely held across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant theology, with differing emphases.

positions.summary: Some readings stress the coming visible reign of God and warn against identifying present political or ecclesial success with the kingdom's fullness. The kingdom's final victory remains God's future act.
positions.traditions: Found in many evangelical and eschatological traditions.

positions.summary: Other approaches stress the kingdom's present ethical and social implications, including justice, mercy, reconciliation and witness, while differing over how directly these should be identified with God's reign.
positions.traditions: Various liberation, evangelical, Catholic social teaching, Anabaptist and missional traditions.

entries.historicalContext: The kingdom was central to Jesus' preaching and has been interpreted in relation to Israel's hope, the church, the Holy Spirit, social ethics and eschatology. Different eras have emphasised its spiritual, institutional, social or future dimensions.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Debates concern the relation of kingdom and church, the extent of present fulfilment, political power, social transformation and the timing and character of final consummation.
entries.readingCaution: Do not equate God's kingdom with any political party, nation or human institution. Hold present discipleship and future hope together, and read Jesus' kingdom teaching in its Gospel context.

entries.title: Original sin, ancestral sin and human brokenness
entries.question: How do Christians understand humanity's inherited condition after the fall?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm that sin has profoundly damaged human life and that every person needs God's grace and redemption in Christ. They agree that death, disordered desire and moral failure are universal realities, while differing in how the consequences of Adam's sin are transmitted and described.

positions.summary: Many Western traditions describe original sin as an inherited condition involving a loss of original righteousness and a deep disorder of human nature. Some traditions, especially in parts of the Reformed stream, also speak of inherited guilt; others distinguish inherited corruption from personal culpability.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed and other Western traditions, with important differences between them.

positions.summary: Orthodox theologians commonly speak of ancestral sin: humanity inherits mortality, corruption and a damaged environment of sin through Adam, but personal guilt is not ordinarily treated as inherited in the same way as Adam's own act. Each person becomes responsible for their own sins.
positions.traditions: Eastern Orthodox theology, while individual theologians explain the inheritance of sin in varied ways.

positions.summary: Many Wesleyan and evangelical accounts affirm that all people are born into a fallen condition and cannot heal themselves apart from grace. They often emphasise prevenient grace and distinguish inherited sinfulness from the guilt of deliberate personal sin.
positions.traditions: Wesleyan, Methodist, Baptist, Pentecostal and other Protestant communities; formulations vary.

entries.historicalContext: Christian reflection on Adam, sin and grace developed through biblical interpretation and debates involving Irenaeus, Augustine, the Eastern Fathers, the Reformation and later Wesleyan theology. The phrase original sin has therefore carried different meanings across traditions.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Disagreement concerns inherited guilt, inherited corruption, mortality, infant baptism, the freedom of the will and how Romans 5 should be read alongside Ezekiel 18. Traditions also differ over the relation between Adam's act and each person's own responsibility.
entries.readingCaution: Read Romans 5:12-21 in its full argument about Adam and Christ, and read Ezekiel 18 alongside it. Do not use inherited-sin teaching to shame children, excuse personal wrongdoing or claim that people are beyond God's grace.

entries.title: Sanctification, holiness and Christian maturity
entries.question: How does a believer grow in holiness, and is complete holiness possible in this life?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm that salvation leads to a transformed life shaped by the Holy Spirit. They call believers to holiness, love, obedience, repentance and ongoing growth, while recognising the need for grace and the reality of human weakness.

positions.summary: Many Reformed and evangelical traditions describe sanctification as the Spirit's continuing work through the Word, prayer, the church, repentance and daily obedience. Growth is real but remains incomplete in this life, with final perfection at glorification.
positions.traditions: Reformed, Baptist, many Anglican and evangelical churches.

positions.summary: Wesleyan-Holiness traditions teach that God can bring believers into a deeper work of grace in which the heart is cleansed from inward sin and filled with perfect love. This is not usually understood as freedom from ignorance, mistakes, temptation or the need for continued growth.
positions.traditions: Wesleyan, Methodist-Holiness and Church of the Nazarene traditions, with differing definitions.

positions.summary: Eastern Orthodox theology often describes growth in holiness as synergy: human response made possible by divine grace, through prayer, repentance, sacramental life and participation in God's life. The goal is transformation and communion with God rather than self-achieved moral perfection.
positions.traditions: Eastern Orthodox churches and related theological streams.

entries.historicalContext: The New Testament uses several images for holiness, including being set apart, growing in virtue, putting off the old self and sharing in God's life. Later debates shaped distinct Protestant accounts of sanctification, especially in Reformed and Wesleyan traditions.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Differences concern whether entire sanctification is possible before death, how to define perfection, the relation of justification and sanctification, the role of sacraments and spiritual disciplines, and how divine grace and human cooperation relate.
entries.readingCaution: Do not equate holiness with flawless performance, emotional intensity or outward rule-keeping. Read commands to holiness alongside the New Testament's teaching on grace, confession, restoration and the fruit of the Spirit.

entries.title: Divorce, remarriage and pastoral care
entries.question: How should churches interpret Jesus' teaching on marriage, divorce and remarriage while caring for people in painful or unsafe situations?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm the seriousness of marriage, the call to faithfulness, the dignity and safety of every person, and the church's responsibility to offer truthful, compassionate pastoral care. They agree that abuse, coercion and abandonment must not be excused or concealed.

positions.view: Restrictive accounts of divorce and remarriage
positions.summary: Some traditions interpret Jesus' teaching as permitting separation or divorce only in narrowly defined circumstances and may restrict remarriage while a former spouse is living. Pastoral practice and the recognition of annulment or separation differ among churches.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic teaching on the indissolubility of a valid sacramental marriage; some conservative Protestant communities hold similarly restrictive positions.

positions.summary: Many Protestant interpreters understand Matthew's exception clause and Paul's teaching about abandonment as allowing divorce, and sometimes remarriage, in specified circumstances such as sexual immorality or desertion. Churches differ over whether abuse falls within these or other grounds.
positions.traditions: Many Anglican, Baptist, Reformed, Methodist, Pentecostal and evangelical churches, with substantial internal diversity.

positions.summary: Some churches emphasise careful discernment, protection from harm, repentance where possible, legal safeguards, counselling and restoration when safe. They may recognise that a marriage covenant has been gravely violated and that pastoral decisions require attention to the whole biblical witness and the person's circumstances.
positions.traditions: Found across several Protestant, Catholic and independent pastoral settings; policies vary.

entries.historicalContext: Christian teaching on marriage developed through Jesus' Gospel sayings, Paul's pastoral counsel and centuries of church discipline and civil law. Different traditions distinguish civil divorce, ecclesial recognition, annulment, separation and permission to remarry in different ways.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Disagreement concerns the meaning of the exception in Matthew, Paul's instruction about an unbelieving spouse, whether abuse constitutes covenant-breaking grounds, the status of remarriage and how church discipline should be applied.
entries.readingCaution: No one should be told to remain in immediate danger or to submit to violence. Prioritise safety, safeguarding, medical and legal support where needed. Do not pressure someone to reconcile with an abuser, and do not make a quick ruling without listening carefully and protecting children.

entries.title: Scripture, tradition and church authority
entries.question: How do the Bible, historic tradition, church teaching and the work of the Holy Spirit relate as sources of Christian authority?
entries.sharedGround: Historic Christian traditions affirm the unique importance of the apostolic witness, the centrality of Scripture, the need for faithful interpretation and the Holy Spirit's guidance of the church. They reject private claims that contradict the gospel and recognise the value of learning from earlier generations.

positions.summary: Many Protestant traditions teach that Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith and practice. Creeds, teachers and church traditions can carry real authority but remain subject to testing by Scripture.
positions.traditions: Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist, evangelical and many Anglican traditions, interpreted in different ways.

positions.summary: Roman Catholic teaching holds that Scripture and apostolic Tradition form one sacred deposit of God's Word, authentically interpreted by the church's teaching office. The Magisterium serves this deposit rather than standing above it.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic Church; official teaching distinguishes Scripture, Tradition and Magisterium.

positions.summary: Eastern Orthodox theology understands Scripture within the living Holy Tradition of the church, including worship, the Fathers, ecumenical councils and the church's continuing life in the Spirit. Scripture remains central within this integrated tradition.
positions.traditions: Eastern Orthodox churches, with varied emphases among theologians.

entries.historicalContext: The early church received apostolic writings, preserved teaching through worship and episcopal oversight, and used councils to address disputes. The Reformation sharpened debates about the final norm of doctrine, while Catholic and Orthodox traditions articulated their accounts of Scripture and Tradition in distinct ways.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Differences concern the canon, the authority and infallibility of councils, the role of bishops and the pope, doctrinal development, the sufficiency of Scripture and how the church recognises authentic apostolic Tradition.
entries.readingCaution: Do not use 'tradition' as a synonym for error or 'the Bible alone' as permission to ignore context, language, history and the wider church. Test teachings carefully, distinguish official doctrine from local custom, and avoid claims of private revelation that override Scripture.

entries.title: Christian faith, government and public life
entries.question: How should Christians relate to civil authority, political power, justice and public responsibility?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm that civil authorities have a role in public order, that rulers are accountable to God, that Christians should seek the good of their neighbours, and that allegiance to God must not be surrendered to unjust human power.

positions.summary: Some Protestant traditions distinguish the church's spiritual mission from the civil authority's task of maintaining public order. Christians may serve in public life while resisting the confusion of the gospel with state power.
positions.traditions: Lutheran and Reformed political theology, though the formulations differ substantially.

positions.view: Christian public engagement and social witness
positions.summary: Other traditions emphasise active participation in civic life to protect human dignity, pursue justice, care for the poor, defend the vulnerable and promote peace. Political action is viewed as one form of neighbour-love, not the fulfilment of God's kingdom.
positions.traditions: Catholic social teaching, many Protestant social-ethics traditions, Anabaptist and evangelical movements, with different methods.

positions.summary: Some Christians understand Jesus' teaching on enemy-love and the New Testament's call to peace as requiring nonviolence, conscientious objection or refusal to participate in war and coercive state violence.
positions.traditions: Historic peace churches such as Mennonite, Brethren and Quaker communities, alongside other Christian pacifists.

entries.historicalContext: Christians have lived under empires, monarchies, democracies and authoritarian governments. The church's approaches have ranged from withdrawal and nonviolence to public office, political advocacy and resistance to unjust laws.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Debates include the limits of obedience to rulers, Christian participation in military service, political advocacy, church-state relations, civil disobedience and how to pursue justice without making a political movement identical with the gospel.
entries.readingCaution: Do not equate any nation, party, leader or policy with the kingdom of God. Romans 13 must be read alongside Acts 5:29 and the prophetic critique of unjust rulers. Reject political coercion, hatred and dehumanisation; protect conscience and the dignity of neighbours.

entries.title: The biblical canon and deuterocanonical books
entries.question: Which writings belong to the Old Testament canon, and how did Christian communities receive and use these books?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm that the Scriptures are authoritative for faith and life and that the canon was received through the worship, teaching and discernment of the people of God. Traditions broadly agree on the central witness of the biblical books while differing over the boundaries and status of several ancient Jewish writings.

positions.summary: Most Protestant traditions receive 39 Old Testament books and 27 New Testament books. The additional Jewish-Greek writings are often called Apocrypha and may be valued for historical or devotional reading, but they are not normally treated as canonical Scripture for establishing doctrine.
positions.traditions: Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal and many other Protestant churches; Anglican and Lutheran histories include varied liturgical use of some Apocrypha.

positions.summary: The Roman Catholic Church receives the deuterocanonical books as part of the Old Testament canon, including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1–2 Maccabees and additions to Esther and Daniel. Catholic teaching connects their reception with the Church's tradition and councils.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic Church; see its official canon lists and teaching on Scripture and Tradition.

positions.view: Eastern Orthodox and other ancient Eastern canons
positions.summary: Eastern Orthodox churches receive a broader Old Testament collection than the Protestant canon, but exact lists and liturgical status can differ among Greek, Slavic and other Orthodox traditions. Other ancient Eastern churches also have their own received canonical collections.
positions.traditions: Eastern Orthodox churches and other ancient Eastern Christian communities; avoid assuming a single identical list across all jurisdictions.

entries.historicalContext: The early church inherited Jewish Scriptures in Hebrew and Greek forms and used a range of writings in worship and instruction. Regional lists and usage developed over centuries; later councils and confessional statements clarified different communities' received canons. The history is more complex than a single late decision by one council.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Christians differ over which ancient Jewish books are canonical, how the Septuagint relates to the Hebrew textual tradition, and how church reception and historical evidence should be weighed. Some traditions distinguish canonical, deuterocanonical and ecclesiastical books in different ways.
entries.readingCaution: Do not claim that every Christian community has always used exactly the same table of contents. Distinguish the status of a book within a tradition from its historical value, and do not use Revelation 22:18-19 as if it directly defined the boundaries of the entire Bible.

entries.title: The person of Christ and the language of two natures
entries.question: How do Christian traditions describe the full divinity and full humanity of Jesus Christ in one person?
entries.sharedGround: Historic Trinitarian Christian traditions affirm that Jesus Christ is truly divine and truly human, the one Son of God incarnate. They reject dividing Christ into two persons or treating His humanity as an illusion, and they confess that His saving work depends on who He is.

positions.summary: Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and many Protestant churches receive the Definition of Chalcedon: Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, without confusion, change, division or separation. The formula protects both His full humanity and full divinity.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and many other churches that receive Chalcedon.

positions.summary: Oriental Orthodox theology commonly speaks of the one united incarnate nature of the Word from two natures, fully divine and fully human. It rejects the confusion or absorption of Christ's humanity and does not intend to teach that Christ is less than fully human or divine.
positions.traditions: Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean and Malankara Orthodox churches; formulations vary among theologians.

positions.summary: Many modern dialogues have found substantial shared confession beneath historic terminology, while recognising that technical differences and church divisions remain significant. Careful explanation distinguishes the intended meaning of a formula from how opponents once described it.
positions.traditions: Bilateral dialogues among Chalcedonian and Oriental Orthodox churches and theologians; not a replacement for each church's official doctrine.

entries.historicalContext: The fourth- and fifth-century debates addressed how the eternal Son is united to the human nature assumed in the incarnation. The Council of Chalcedon in 451 produced a widely received definition, while Oriental Orthodox churches did not receive that council's formulation. Subsequent dialogue has clarified areas of agreement and remaining questions.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Differences concern the preferred technical language for the union of divinity and humanity, the reception of particular councils and how to interpret earlier theologians. Avoid equating miaphysitism with Eutychianism or assuming every church uses identical terminology.
entries.readingCaution: Begin with the biblical witness to Jesus' identity and saving work. Do not reduce the debate to slogans such as 'two persons' versus 'one nature'; represent each tradition using its own careful self-description.

entries.title: Israel, the Church and covenant fulfilment
entries.question: How do Christians understand the relationship between God's promises to Israel and the identity and mission of the Church?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm God's faithfulness to His promises, the centrality of Jesus the Messiah and the inclusion of Gentiles in God's saving purpose. Romans 9–11 warns Gentile believers against arrogance and insists that God's gifts and calling are not treated casually.

positions.summary: Many covenant theologians emphasise the continuity of God's one gracious purpose through successive covenants, fulfilled in Christ and shared by Jews and Gentiles in one people of God. They differ on how particular promises to ethnic Israel are fulfilled and whether any future national restoration is expected.
positions.traditions: Reformed, Presbyterian and some Anglican and Baptist theologians; there is internal diversity.

positions.summary: Dispensational theologians commonly distinguish Israel and the Church within God's unfolding plan and expect particular Old Testament promises to Israel to have a future fulfilment for the Jewish people. Progressive forms also emphasise the inaugurated kingdom and fulfilment in Christ.
positions.traditions: Classical and progressive dispensational communities, especially in some evangelical churches; views vary.

positions.view: Progressive covenantal and other mediating approaches
positions.summary: Some theologians stress the progressive fulfilment of the covenants in Christ while retaining a future significance for ethnic Israel or resisting a simple replacement model. They seek to read the whole canon without collapsing every promise into one undifferentiated category.
positions.traditions: Progressive covenantal, new covenant and other evangelical approaches; terminology is not uniform.

entries.historicalContext: The New Testament interprets Israel's Scriptures in light of Jesus and the inclusion of Gentiles. Early disputes about circumcision and Torah observance are addressed in Acts 15 and Galatians. Later Christian history includes both theological debates and serious anti-Jewish misuse of Scripture, which must be acknowledged.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Traditions differ over covenant continuity, the meaning of Israel in Romans 9–11, land promises, the future of ethnic Israel and how prophetic texts relate to the Church. They also debate how to distinguish biblical theological claims from modern political positions.
entries.readingCaution: Do not use a theological position to justify antisemitism or to equate modern political policies automatically with biblical prophecy. Read Romans 11 in full and heed Paul's warning against boasting over the branches.

entries.title: The Mosaic Law and Christian obedience
entries.question: How should Christians understand the continuing authority and application of the Law given to Israel?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm that the Old Testament is Scripture and that Jesus fulfils God's purposes. They agree that believers are called to holiness, love of neighbour and obedience shaped by Christ, while differing on how the Mosaic covenant's commands apply to the Church.

positions.summary: Lutheran theology often distinguishes the Law, which exposes sin and guides civil life and Christian conduct, from the Gospel, which announces God's promise in Christ. The distinction is not simply Old Testament versus New Testament; both Law and Gospel can be found throughout Scripture.
positions.traditions: Lutheran churches and theologians; explanations of the Law's third use vary.

positions.view: Reformed moral, civil and ceremonial distinctions
positions.summary: Many Reformed theologians distinguish moral commands, civil laws for Israel's historic polity and ceremonial laws fulfilled in Christ. The moral law continues to instruct Christian life, while civil and ceremonial provisions are not applied unchanged to modern states or churches.
positions.traditions: Reformed and Presbyterian traditions, with varied confessional formulations.

positions.summary: New Covenant theologians emphasise that believers are not under the Mosaic covenant as a covenant code but are called to the law of Christ. Wesleyan traditions stress grace-enabled holiness and love, reading Old Testament commands through Christ and the New Testament's moral teaching.
positions.traditions: New Covenant, Wesleyan and many evangelical traditions; internal differences remain.

entries.historicalContext: The question became especially urgent in the early Church when Gentile believers joined communities rooted in Israel's Scriptures. Acts 15, Galatians and Hebrews address circumcision, covenant identity, sacrifice and the fulfilment of promises in Christ. Later Protestant traditions developed different ways of describing continuity and discontinuity.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Christians differ over the status of the Sabbath, food laws, tithing, civil legislation, the moral law and the meaning of 'fulfil' in Matthew 5. Some distinctions are theological frameworks rather than labels explicitly used by the biblical authors.
entries.readingCaution: Do not tell Christians that the Old Testament is irrelevant, nor impose Israel's covenant code unchanged on the Church. Read commands in their covenant, literary and historical settings and follow how the New Testament applies them.

entries.title: The intermediate state and the hope of resurrection
entries.question: What happens between death and the final resurrection according to Christian interpretations of Scripture?
entries.sharedGround: Historic Christian traditions affirm that death does not defeat God's promise and that the final Christian hope includes resurrection and judgment. They differ over the condition of the dead before the resurrection, but the final resurrection remains central to the New Testament's hope.

positions.summary: Many Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions understand believers who die as consciously with Christ while awaiting the resurrection of the body. They appeal to passages such as Philippians 1 and 2 Corinthians 5, while acknowledging that the intermediate state is not described in exhaustive detail.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Reformed, Methodist and many evangelical churches.

positions.summary: Some Christians understand death as an unconscious state until the resurrection, often using the biblical metaphor of sleep and emphasising that immortality is God's gift rather than an inherent human possession. They read passages about being with Christ in light of the final resurrection hope.
positions.traditions: Some Adventist, conditionalist and other Protestant theologians; views vary within these communities.

entries.historicalContext: Early Christian teaching strongly emphasised bodily resurrection, while theologians also discussed the soul's condition after death. Later debates about immortality, resurrection and the meaning of 'sleep' developed within different philosophical and biblical frameworks.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: The main questions concern whether the dead are conscious before resurrection, how to interpret 'sleep' language, and the relation between body and soul. Traditions also differ on prayer for the departed and purification after death, treated in a separate comparison.
entries.readingCaution: Do not let debates about the intermediate state obscure the clear New Testament promise of resurrection. Read each passage in context and avoid claiming that one short text answers every question about the afterlife.

entries.title: Spiritual warfare, deliverance and pastoral discernment
entries.question: How should Christians understand demonic oppression, prayer for deliverance and the limits of spiritual explanations?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm that Scripture portrays spiritual evil as real and that Christ's authority is greater. They also affirm prayer, truth, pastoral care and the need to protect vulnerable people. The existence of spiritual conflict does not make every illness, trauma or hardship a demonic event.

positions.summary: Many Pentecostal and charismatic communities expect prayer for deliverance and spiritual gifts to remain active in the Church. They may use focused prayer, pastoral discernment and communal support, while responsible ministries insist on consent, accountability and referral for medical or mental-health needs.
positions.traditions: Pentecostal, charismatic and some renewal movements; practice varies widely.

positions.summary: Some Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant communities maintain formal prayers or rites of exorcism under trained oversight, while warning against sensationalism and untrained intervention. They stress sacramental life, confession, prayer and careful assessment rather than assuming every problem has a demonic cause.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox pastoral practice, and cautious evangelical traditions; policies differ.

positions.summary: Many Christian counsellors and pastors emphasise that spiritual care and appropriate medical or psychological treatment need not compete. They resist diagnosing people from a distance and prioritise safety, informed consent, safeguarding and qualified clinical assessment when symptoms require it.
positions.traditions: Cross-denominational pastoral, chaplaincy and clinical approaches; not a separate creed.

entries.historicalContext: The Gospels describe Jesus confronting unclean spirits, while the New Testament also addresses suffering, illness, temptation and communal care in distinct ways. Christian communities developed different pastoral practices, from formal rites to spontaneous prayer, within changing cultural understandings of mental and physical illness.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Christians differ over the frequency and forms of demonic activity, whether contemporary deliverance ministries should be expected, the role of formal rites and how spiritual discernment relates to medicine and psychology.
entries.readingCaution: Never tell someone to stop prescribed treatment, submit to frightening or coercive rituals, or interpret abuse, disability or mental illness as proof of demonic possession. Any ministry must respect consent, safety, safeguarding and professional care.

entries.title: Christian pacifism, just war and peacebuilding
entries.question: When, if ever, may Christians participate in war or use force to protect others?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm the value of human life, the call to love enemies, the pursuit of peace and the duty to protect neighbours from grave harm. They agree that violence is morally serious and must never be celebrated or used for selfish gain.

positions.summary: Pacifist traditions interpret Jesus' commands to love enemies and reject retaliation as a call for Christians to refuse participation in war and to practise nonviolent resistance, reconciliation and enemy-love even under threat.
positions.traditions: Anabaptist, Mennonite, Quaker and other Christian pacifist communities; pacifist convictions also appear within wider traditions.

positions.summary: Just war traditions hold that force may sometimes be morally permitted to defend the innocent or restrain grave aggression, but only under strict conditions such as just cause, legitimate authority, last resort, proportionality and protection of noncombatants.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Reformed and other traditions with varied applications and critiques.

positions.summary: Some theologians emphasise peacebuilding, prevention, restorative justice and nonviolent alternatives while recognising difficult questions about protecting people from immediate violence. They may critique both absolute pacifism and easy appeals to just war.
positions.traditions: Ecumenical peace movements and theologians across several traditions.

entries.historicalContext: The early Church included strong nonviolent witness, while later Christian societies developed theories of legitimate public force. The rise of Christian empires, modern nation-states and international law shaped later debates about war, conscience and protection of civilians.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Disagreements concern whether force can ever be compatible with discipleship, how Romans 13 relates to enemy-love, who may authorise war and whether just-war criteria can be met in modern conflict.
entries.readingCaution: Do not use Romans 13 to excuse atrocities or Matthew 5 to dismiss the urgent protection of victims. Examine evidence, civilian harm, alternatives and the moral responsibility of every actor; never sanctify a nation or military campaign as automatically God's cause.

entries.title: Prayer for the departed and purgatory
entries.question: Do Christians pray for the dead, and how do traditions understand purification after death?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm God's justice and mercy, the final resurrection and the hope that the dead remain within God's care. They differ over whether prayer for the departed is appropriate and whether there is a post-death purification for those who die in God's grace.

positions.summary: Catholic teaching describes purgatory as the final purification of those who die in God's grace and friendship but remain imperfectly purified. It is not a second chance after death or an alternative to Christ's saving work; prayer for the departed is part of the communion of saints.
positions.traditions: Roman Catholic Church; consult official teaching for its precise definition.

positions.view: Eastern Orthodox prayer for the departed
positions.summary: Orthodox churches pray for those who have died and entrust them to God's mercy, but do not define the intermediate state using the same detailed dogmatic account of purgatory as Roman Catholic teaching. Orthodox theologians differ in how they explain post-death purification.
positions.traditions: Eastern Orthodox churches; local liturgical and theological emphases vary.

positions.summary: Many Protestant traditions reject purgatory as insufficiently grounded in their received biblical canon and emphasise Christ's completed work and the final judgment. Most do not practise prayer for the dead as a means of assisting their state, though some Anglican and Lutheran contexts have varied historical practices.
positions.traditions: Reformed, Baptist, evangelical and many other Protestant communities; practice and confessional language differ.

entries.historicalContext: Prayer for the departed appears in ancient Christian practice, while formal explanations of purification developed over time. The Reformation challenged purgatory, indulgences and related practices; Catholic teaching was clarified at the Council of Trent, while Orthodox traditions retained prayer for the departed without adopting the same definition.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Debates include the interpretation of 1 Corinthians 3, the status of early Christian practice, the nature of purification, the authority of church tradition and whether prayers can benefit the departed.
entries.readingCaution: Do not claim that one cited passage directly states every later doctrine. Explain how each tradition interprets the texts and distinguish official teaching from popular descriptions or speculative imagery.

entries.title: The scope of salvation: exclusivism, inclusivism and universalism
entries.question: How do Christians understand the possibility and scope of salvation through Jesus Christ?
entries.sharedGround: Historic Christian traditions confess that salvation is grounded in God's grace and the person and work of Jesus Christ. They also affirm the Church's call to proclaim the gospel, pray for all people and entrust final judgment to God's justice and mercy.

positions.summary: Many Christians hold that explicit faith in Jesus Christ is ordinarily necessary for salvation and stress the urgency of evangelism. Within this broad view, theologians differ on how God judges those who have never heard the gospel or are unable to respond in ordinary ways.
positions.traditions: Many evangelical, Reformed, Baptist and other Protestant traditions, alongside particularist voices in other churches.

positions.summary: Inclusivist theologians maintain that any salvation is entirely through Christ, while allowing that God's grace may reach people who do not possess explicit Christian knowledge or membership. They often appeal to God's universal desire to save and the limits of human knowledge about individual judgment.
positions.traditions: Some Catholic, Anglican and Protestant theologians; official formulations and boundaries differ.

positions.summary: Some Christians hope that God's reconciling purpose will finally embrace all people; a smaller number argue that all will certainly be saved. Others reject dogmatic universalism while praying and hoping for the widest possible mercy.
positions.traditions: A minority of theologians across historical traditions; hopeful universalism and dogmatic universalism should not be conflated.

entries.historicalContext: Christian reflection has held together biblical passages about the uniqueness of Christ, the universal scope of God's saving will, judgment and the hope of reconciliation. Different theologians weigh these texts and the authority of later church teaching in different ways.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: The debate concerns the necessity of explicit faith, the destiny of those who have not heard the gospel, the meaning of universal reconciliation texts and whether final judgment is everlasting, remedial or otherwise. Traditions also distinguish hope from a doctrine asserted with certainty.
entries.readingCaution: Do not declare specific individuals saved or condemned. Present the biblical texts in context, distinguish official teaching from theological speculation, and never use the debate to discourage evangelism, compassion or respect for people of other faiths.

entries.title: Christian unity, ecumenism and denominational identity
entries.question: How should Christians pursue visible unity while remaining faithful to doctrinal convictions?
entries.sharedGround: Christian traditions affirm the unity of Christ's body and the call to love, humility and mutual service. They also recognise that serious disagreements about doctrine, sacraments, authority and ministry cannot be resolved by pretending they do not exist.

positions.summary: Ecumenical movements seek visible Christian unity through dialogue, shared prayer, cooperation and theological agreements. Many distinguish essential doctrines from matters that can be held with diversity, while recognising that sacramental and authority questions remain difficult.
positions.traditions: World Council of Churches member traditions, Catholic and Orthodox dialogues, Anglican and Protestant ecumenical bodies; participation varies.

positions.summary: Confessional traditions emphasise that unity must be grounded in truth and shared teaching, not only institutional cooperation. They may cooperate in service while maintaining separate church structures where disagreements about the gospel, sacraments or authority remain unresolved.
positions.traditions: Reformed, Lutheran, Baptist, evangelical, Catholic and Orthodox communities in differing ways; no tradition is internally uniform.

positions.summary: Some churches prioritise local congregational responsibility and voluntary networks, viewing unity as spiritual fellowship and shared mission without requiring one global governing structure. They may welcome cooperation while preserving local doctrinal accountability.
positions.traditions: Many Baptist, independent evangelical and congregational churches; arrangements differ.

entries.historicalContext: The New Testament addresses divisions in local churches and describes major disputes resolved through communal discernment, as in Acts 15. Later history includes schisms, councils, reform movements and modern ecumenical efforts seeking reconciliation while acknowledging unresolved differences.
entries.areasOfDisagreement: Christians differ over the nature of visible unity, the authority needed to settle disputes, sacramental recognition, ordained ministry and whether doctrinal agreement is a prerequisite for shared worship or communion.
entries.readingCaution: Do not treat every denominational difference as trivial, nor use disagreement as an excuse for contempt. Distinguish cooperation in service, theological dialogue, shared prayer and full ecclesial communion; each involves different commitments.
